headline: A symbolic checker that examines one output location for every input, instead of every output for one input, found real bugs in 600 of 6,988 machine-written CUDA kernels that differential testing had already passed.

items.title: Threshold spread of 41 mV is what makes a dot array addressable
items.dek: Quobly and STMicroelectronics cooled quantum dots made on ST's commercial 300-millimetre line in Crolles to about 2 kelvin, and across 546 measurements the gate voltage at which a dot captures its first electron landed within ±35 millivolts on the 377 that worked.
items.why_it_matters: A spin qubit is one electron trapped under a gate, so every dot in an array has to be emptied and then loaded to exactly one electron before any quantum operation begins. When that loading voltage differs by hundreds of millivolts between neighbours, each dot needs its own tuning run, and tuning time is what has held these arrays in the tens of devices. A ±35 mV spread means one voltage, or a coarse map, can address a whole array.
items.background_md: A silicon spin qubit stores a bit in the orientation of one electron's magnetic moment, which first requires a potential well small enough that admitting a second electron costs more energy than the control voltages supply. That well is made by gate electrodes over a narrow silicon channel — the same structure a MOSFET uses, which is why such devices can be built on a production CMOS line at all. The inheritance brings the line's oldest problem with it: threshold voltage scatters between nominally identical devices because oxide thickness, interface charge and edge roughness scatter, and an array of dots feels that scatter as every dot wanting a different voltage.
items.deeper_md:
Measured against ST's standard 28 nm FD-SOI on the same benches, the dedicated QSOI flow moves three numbers. Threshold-voltage standard deviation across 28 dies at room temperature falls from 385 mV to 41.1 mV; subthreshold swing goes from 193 ± 155 to 104 ± 10 mV/dec; the back-gate tuning factor drops from −1013 to −347 mV/V and barrier-via coupling from −491 to −64.6 mV/V. Those last two are the electrostatic version of the same sentence the σ is making: the plunger gate now controls its own dot instead of sharing control with everything nearby.

The devices are silicon nanowires defined by shallow trench isolation, carrying plunger gates, tungsten-via barrier gates and a back gate, with a single-electron transistor reading charge beside each row. 377 of 546 charge-stability maps show a detectable first electron — 69 percent — and the authors say plainly that part of the shortfall is detector sensitivity and the spacing between the sensor and the dot, not missing dots.

The number to hold it against: imec reported threshold-voltage σ down to 63 mV across 392 dots in a 7 × 7 array on a 300 mm EUV line, with a non-monotonic dependence on oxide thickness. Different quantity, different temperature, so the two are not a ranking.

glossary.definition: The standard deviation of threshold voltage across nominally identical devices — the number that says how far apart two transistors from one wafer will switch on. Here it falls from 385 mV to 41.1 mV.
The gate voltage needed to change a transistor's off-state current tenfold; room temperature puts a floor near 60 mV/decade, and a wide spread in it means the channel is not uniformly controlled.
An island between two tunnel barriers whose current responds to nearby charge, placed next to a quantum dot so it can report when one electron enters without the dot carrying current itself.
The gate whose voltage sets how deep a dot's potential well is, and so how many electrons sit in it; barrier gates either side set how easily electrons tunnel in and out.

items.fab_angle: This is a mismatch result before it is a quantum one, and mismatch is the constraint MNF hits on the design side: the standard deviation of threshold voltage falls as 1/√(WL), so analog area is bought from statistics rather than from lithography. A number like 41.1 mV is what a line reports when it has stopped losing that argument.

items.title: Charge the gate slowly enough and the capacitor gives the energy back
items.dek: Franciszek Łukowski, Maciej Pyrzowski and Aida Todri-Sanial simulated positive-feedback adiabatic logic — gates powered by a ramping clock instead of a fixed supply, so charge put onto an output is pulled back into the source rather than dumped to ground — in TSMC's 16-nanometre FinFET process, and found a triangular ramp beats a sine.
items.why_it_matters: Energy recovery has always been priced out by its own clock: a conventional gate spends about ½CV² per transition no matter how fast it switches, while an adiabatic gate spends roughly (RC/T)CV², so the saving is bought entirely with transition time T and every nanosecond of T is throughput surrendered. Two things in these papers move that trade — FinFET RC products are now small enough that the ratio still favours recovery at 7.94 GHz, and the power clock is built from an on-chip oscillator instead of assumed ideal.
items.background_md: Every time a CMOS gate switches, it charges its output capacitance through a transistor channel and then shorts that charge to ground. Half the energy drawn from the supply, ½CV², is burned in the channel resistance on the way up and the other half on the way down, and the total is independent of how quickly you do it. Adiabatic logic replaces the fixed supply with a clock that ramps, so the charging current — and with it the I²R loss — falls as the ramp is stretched. The dissipated energy then goes as (RC/T)CV², which has no floor, only a time cost.
items.deeper_md:
The headline device number is an energy-delay product: 1.23 × 10⁻²⁶ J·s for a low-threshold Buffer/NOT cell at a 0.6 V clock amplitude and 7.94 GHz, with roughly 5× the energy benefit over static CMOS appearing at lower frequencies and higher supplies. Three loss mechanisms are named and none of them is the ramp: threshold-voltage drop, charging of the complementary output node that dual-rail logic then discards, and the depth of the PFAL logic tree itself.

The companion paper varies the waveform. A triangular power clock wins, giving up to 3.83× lower energy than the equivalent static CMOS gate, with sinusoidal excitation up to 1.32× better than trapezoidal; a 4-bit Brent–Kung carry-lookahead adder reaches up to 5.3× on the triangular clock. The generator is the part usually waved away, and here it is a parallel-coupled quadrature VCO: Buffer/NOT energy stays within 2 percent of the ideal-sinusoid case at 3 GHz.

All of it is simulation in a 16 nm PDK, and the comparison is against a static-CMOS estimate rather than a measured part. For scale, Yin and Stan's adiabatic MAC systolic array in the same 16 nm class reports 42 percent core and 36 percent system power reduction at 1 GHz — far short of 3.83×, because a system number has to carry the clock generator and everything that is not adiabatic.

glossary.definition: In adiabatic logic, the supply and the clock are the same ramping waveform: it charges the gate's output on the way up and recovers that charge on the way down, so its shape sets the energy bill.
Energy per operation multiplied by the delay of that operation, in joule-seconds. It exists because energy alone can always be improved by going slower, which adiabatic logic does by construction.

A style that computes a signal and its complement on two separate nodes. Adiabatic families need it to guarantee a discharge path, and it means one of the two output nodes is charged and then thrown away every cycle.
A parallel-prefix adder that trades a longer critical path for far fewer internal nodes than Kogge-Stone; the sparse structure is why it appears in low-energy designs.

items.title: A potassium hydroxide etch makes the mirror that feeds a photonic chip
items.dek: Hamdy Elshehaby and three co-authors propose getting light from an optical fibre into a silicon chip by bouncing it off a 54.7-degree silicon facet that a potassium hydroxide etch produces on its own, and simulate 88 percent transmission — 0.56 decibels of loss — at 1,550 nanometres.
items.why_it_matters: Optical input to a chip is limited by channel density rather than by loss: a conventional edge coupler puts every fibre on one line along the chip edge, at the 127-micrometre pitch a V-groove fibre array enforces. Reflecting off an internal facet moves the coupling region from a line to an area, so channels can stack in two dimensions and the interface sits under the chip instead of competing with back-end metal routing. The simulated ±2 micrometre vertical tolerance is the number that decides whether assembly can be passive.
items.background_md: A silicon waveguide confines light in a cross-section a few hundred nanometres across; a standard single-mode fibre carries a mode roughly ten micrometres wide. Butt them together and most of the light misses, so an edge coupler spends a few hundred micrometres of chip narrowing the waveguide until its mode expands to meet the fibre. Grating couplers take the other route, diffracting light up out of the surface, and pay for it in bandwidth and polarisation sensitivity. Either way the number of fibres a chip can accept is set by mechanical pitch, and that is the wall co-packaged optics walks into.
items.deeper_md:
The geometry is the argument. Light enters through a cavity wet-etched into the silicon and strikes a {111} sidewall, which stands at 54.7° to a (100) surface because crystallography puts it there — potassium hydroxide attacks {111} planes far more slowly than {100}, so the angle is a property of the material rather than a tolerance to be held. Total internal reflection turns the beam into the plane of the chip, and a wedged buried-oxide ridge shapes the evanescent transfer into the waveguide across a two-dimensional region instead of a single facet line.

The simulated numbers: 88 percent peak coupling (−0.56 dB) at 1550 nm, an 86.45 nm 1-dB bandwidth covering the C-band, ±2 µm vertical and up to 5 µm transverse offset tolerance, ±0.8° angular.

The caveat is the whole status of the work — these are finite-difference time-domain predictions, and nothing has been fabricated or measured. What a built coupler faces is visible in Avdeev's tutorial: −0.15 dB per connection with a high-numerical-aperture UHNA-7 fibre, but −1.50 dB with an ordinary single-mode fibre on the same 220 × 1200 nm waveguide. For alignment budget, Weninger's graded-index coupler measures below 0.27 dB with ±2.38 µm vertical tolerance, so the tolerance claimed here is in the range something already built achieves.

glossary.definition: Ten times the base-10 logarithm of transmitted over incident power; 0.56 dB is 88 percent through, 3 dB is half, and the logarithmic scale is why a fraction of a decibel is worth arguing about.

The width of the optical field a fibre or waveguide actually carries, about 10 µm for standard single-mode fibre at 1550 nm against a few hundred nanometres for a silicon wire — the mismatch every coupler exists to bridge.

The most densely packed crystal planes in silicon, with one dangling bond per surface atom. Alkaline etchants remove them far more slowly than other orientations, so a wet etch on a (100) wafer stops on them at a fixed 54.7°.

Transferring light between two guides by overlapping the exponentially decaying tail of one mode with the other, rather than by pointing one at the other; it works over a region, which is what lets the coupling area be two-dimensional.

items.fab_angle: The unusual thing here is that the precision element is a beaker process. A 54.7° facet needs a hot alkaline bath, a nitride or oxide mask and a (100) wafer, not a lithography tool — which puts the hard part of this structure inside what a teaching cleanroom can already do, and puts the difficulty back on the buried-oxide wedge and the alignment fixture instead.

items.title: Turn microscaling inside out: one mantissa, an exponent per element
items.dek: Yuan Liao and Jae-sun Seo inverted the block number format behind four-bit AI inference — instead of 32 numbers sharing one exponent, eight share a three-bit mantissa and each carries its own exponent — which turns the multiplier array of a vision-language accelerator into a bank of bit shifters.
items.why_it_matters: Shared-exponent formats fail in a specific, locatable way: one large value drags the block's exponent up and everything small in that block underflows to zero, and the paper measures 38.3 percent of the Key matrix underflowing in layer 27 of Qwen2-VL under MXFP4. Inverting which field is shared removes that failure mode, and because a shared mantissa factors straight out of a dot product it removes the multipliers as well — 56,125 µm² of array against 70,391 µm² for an NVFP4 array of the same throughput.
items.background_md: Four bits cannot span the dynamic range of a neural network's activations, so every deployed low-precision format stores numbers in blocks that share a scale factor. OCP's MXFP4 puts 32 elements under one power-of-two exponent; NVIDIA's NVFP4 puts 16 under an eight-bit floating-point scale plus a per-tensor FP32 scalar. The shared field is what makes such a format cheap in memory and in silicon, and it is also the single point of failure, because every element is quantised relative to whatever the largest member of its block demands.
items.deeper_md:
The 4.5-bit variant packs a 32-element block as one 4-bit global maximum exponent, four sub-blocks of eight elements each holding a 3-bit shared mantissa, and per element a sign bit plus a 3-bit relative exponent offset: 144 bits over 32 elements. Reconstruction is x̂ᵢ = (−1)^sᵢ (1.m_shared)₂ × 2^(E_max − Δeᵢ). Because the mantissa is common to the sub-block, the dot product factors — right-shift each weight mantissa by the activation's Δeᵢ, sum in an integer adder tree, and do a single multiply by the shared mantissa at the end. That is why the multipliers disappear.

Synthesised in 28 nm at 500 MHz with 512 MACs per cycle: 56,125 µm², 31.8 mW, 9.1 TOPS/mm² and 16.1 TOPS/W, against 70,391 µm² and 14.0 TOPS/W for NVFP4. End to end it reports 2.3–4.5× speedup and 1.4–2.9× lower energy than the Focus accelerator. Accuracy over six vision-language benchmarks on Qwen2-VL-7B averages 69.3 percent against 69.7 for NVFP4 and 66.8 for MXFP4 at group size 16.

The authors state the limit themselves: on text-only language models MiX trails NVFP4 by 1.3 to 4 points. It buys dynamic range with precision, and that trade only pays where the range is wide — vision tokens span roughly 34× the dynamic range of text tokens.

glossary.definition: A number format in which a fixed-size block of low-precision elements shares one scale factor, so the memory cost per element stays small while the block as a whole can reach an FP32-like exponent range.
Shorthand for a float's field widths: E2M1 is two exponent bits and one mantissa bit plus a sign, the four-bit element; E8M0 is eight exponent bits and no mantissa, a pure power-of-two scale factor.

What happens when a value is too small to represent and becomes zero. In a block format it is caused by a neighbour rather than by the value itself, because the block's shared exponent is set by its largest member.

Tera-operations per second per watt and per square millimetre — the two efficiency numbers an inference datapath is judged on, and the pair a format change moves in opposite directions if it costs precision.

items.title: Posit's exact accumulator is 1,024 bits; break the carry chain up
items.dek: Mario Alonso, Miguel Ángel Sacristán, Guillermo Botella and Alberto Del Barrio replaced the single 1,024-bit fixed-point register that makes posit-64 dot products exact with 32 separate fragments whose carries cross between them on later cycles, and closed the unit at 0.5 nanoseconds in a TSMC 28-nanometre library.
items.why_it_matters: An exact dot product is a real guarantee — rounding happens once, at the end, so the answer no longer depends on the order the terms were added — and it is paid for with one adder as wide as the whole accumulator, whose carry chain then sets the clock period for everything around it. Fragmenting the register converts a worst-case carry propagation paid every cycle into an average one paid only when an accumulation ends, which is what lets exact accumulation run at the frequency of the inexact kind.
items.background_md: Floating-point addition is not associative: because each add rounds, summing the same numbers in a different order gives a different answer, which is why changing a reduction order on a GPU changes a result. Posit arithmetic answers this with a quire, a fixed-point register wide enough to hold every product a dot product can generate without rounding any of them, so the sum is exact and order stops mattering. The width follows from the format's extremes rather than from a design choice, and that width is the entire cost of the guarantee.
items.deeper_md:
Under the 2022 standard with es = 2 the quire is 16n bits wide for an n-bit posit: 512 bits for posit32, 1,024 for posit64, from 2 × (2 × maxE) plus a carry bit with maxE = (n − 2)·2^es. The multispeculative adder splits those N_q bits into N_q/w fragments of width w. During accumulation, carries that cross a fragment boundary are held and applied on a later cycle rather than rippling the full width in one; when the accumulation finishes the unit enters a speculation phase with a static zero prediction and keeps cycling until no inter-fragment carries remain, bounded at N_q/w − 1 cycles.

The multiplier is Booth-4 with Kogge-Stone adders, synthesised against a 0.5 ns constraint. For posit64 with Brent-Kung fragments at w = 32: 48,423 µm², 8.7 percent smaller than the monolithic version, 87.24 mW, 15.8 percent lower power, and 40 chained MACs in 24.22 ns for 2,128.92 pJ. Against 64-bit quire-enabled alternatives the reported cycle time falls by up to 79 percent and area by up to 19.8 percent.

The authors name the limits. Below about four MACs the speculation phase dominates and there is no gain; at w = 2 the design burns more energy than a monolithic adder; no fragment width minimises area and energy together; and the multiplier, not the accumulator, is now the critical path. The wider caveat is that posits ship in no general-purpose CPU, so every baseline here is another posit design.

glossary.definition: A fixed-point accumulator defined by the posit standard, wide enough that any sequence of products can be summed into it with no rounding at all; the result is rounded back to a posit only once, at the end.
The property that (a+b)+c equals a+(b+c). Floating point lacks it because every intermediate result is rounded, which is why two runs of the same reduction in different orders can disagree.

Guessing the carry into a segment of an adder rather than waiting for it, so segments can compute in parallel; a wrong guess costs extra cycles, so the guess here is a static zero with a bounded penalty.
A multiplier technique that recodes the multiplier three bits at a time, roughly halving the number of partial products to be summed and so shortening the adder tree behind them.

items.title: Check one output location for all inputs, not all outputs for one input
items.dek: Paul Biberstein, Joseph Devietti and Mayur Naik ran a symbolic checker over 6,988 machine-written CUDA kernels that differential testing had already marked correct, and found real bugs in 600 of them by inverting the question that testing asks.
items.why_it_matters: Differential testing draws a handful of random tensors from an input space it cannot cover, so a kernel that is wrong only when two values stand in some particular relation passes cleanly. The finding that makes the inverted question cheap is that wrongness is not rare across the output: of 226 confirmed miscomputations, 218 were exposed by the very first output location examined, and all but 13 were present at every location sampled. One location is usually the whole check.
items.background_md: A GPU kernel is normally checked by running it and a reference implementation on the same random tensors and comparing the results. That is cheap, and it is what every kernel-generation benchmark uses, but it inherits the weakness of all testing: it samples a space it cannot enumerate. A tensor kernel's input space is every real-valued tensor of the declared shape, and the errors that survive random sampling are exactly those needing a coincidence between values — an index that only leaves its bounds when a dimension is one, a reduction that only drops a term when two entries cancel.
items.deeper_md:
Thread and block identifiers are treated as symbolic values, so one symbolic execution stands in for an unbounded number of physical GPU threads. The pipeline traces reference and optimised executions, merges them and trims the operations they share, lowers the CUDA and PyTorch operators through PTX into symbolic expressions, and then asks the Z3 SMT solver for a counterexample at a single output location.

The corpus is the AI CUDA Engineer archive's KernelBench level-2 solutions: 6,988 kernels, every one already passed by differential testing. 600 bugs came out, 8.6 percent — 374 caught during symbolic execution as synchronisation or memory-safety violations, 226 as genuinely wrong arithmetic. All 226 were confirmed by replaying the counterexample on a GPU, so the false-positive rate is zero by construction. Execution timed out at 120 seconds with a median of 0.6, checking at 240, and 97.3 percent of bugs surfaced inside two minutes.

The gap the authors flag is the one that matters most here: floating-point values are modelled as reals, so non-associativity and precision loss are invisible — and that is precisely the class of bug a kernel written for speed introduces. On top of that, 1,872 of the 6,988 programs (26.8 percent) use PTX instructions the tool does not support, including __syncwarp and __ballot_sync; 1,175 more time out; and 221 reported inequivalences could not be verified at all, which may be modelling gaps rather than bugs. Full verification rather than bug-finding finished inside an hour for only 58 percent of the programs checked.

glossary.definition: Running two implementations on the same inputs and comparing outputs to decide whether one is correct. It can only ever say that the inputs tried agreed, which is why a coincidence-dependent bug survives it.
Running a program with variables standing in for concrete values, so one run describes every input at once; the result is a formula over those variables rather than a number.

A tool such as Z3 that decides whether a logical formula over arithmetic, arrays and bit-vectors can be satisfied, and if so produces the assignment — here, the concrete tensor that makes two kernels disagree.

NVIDIA's virtual instruction set, sitting between CUDA source and the native machine code a GPU runs. Lowering to it is what lets a checker reason about a kernel without re-implementing CUDA's semantics.

items.title: Only a quarter of the layers can look ahead, and diffusion still works
items.dek: Six researchers converted Qwen3.5 — a model in which three recurrent gated-delta-net layers sit between every full-attention layer — into a diffusion language model that fills masked positions in any order, by unmasking the attention layers only and leaving the recurrent ones strictly causal.
items.why_it_matters: A diffusion language model predicts a masked position from context on both sides of it, which is why every one built so far has rested on full attention: a recurrence carries state forward and has no way to see right. The result here is that most of the layers do not need to. With only the 25 percent that are attention made bidirectional, the hybrid reaches a given training loss in about half the tokens a full-attention control needs — and the recurrent layers are the ones whose cost does not grow with sequence length.
items.background_md: An autoregressive language model emits one token at a time, left to right, and its cost per token grows with the context it attends over. A diffusion language model starts instead from a fully masked sequence and unmasks positions across several passes, so many tokens are decided at once — which requires every position to be predicted from what lies on both sides of it. Hybrid architectures attack the cost from the other direction, replacing most attention layers with linear recurrences that carry a fixed-size state forward. The two ideas pull against each other, because a recurrence is causal by construction.
items.deeper_md:
Qwen3.5 interleaves three Gated DeltaNet layers per attention layer, in 18+6 and 24+8 configurations. Bidirectionalisation is done by the cheapest available route: disable the causal masks on the attention layers and leave the recurrent layers untouched, so about a quarter of the sequence-processing layers can see forward. Training runs 50B and 100B tokens (25k and 50k steps) on a linear masking schedule αₜ = 1 − t with uniform time sampling, over a mixture of 50 percent code, 35 percent general text and 15 percent mathematics, at scales of 0.8B, 2B, 4B and 9B parameters.

The comparison worth reading is token efficiency rather than the leaderboard. dQwen3.5-9B trained on 50B tokens is best on four of seven benchmarks against Dream-7B at 580B tokens, Dream-Coder-7B at 322B and LLaDA-8B at 2.3T. Decoding behaviour stays diffusion-like locally — local AR-ness about 0.64, inside the 0.58–0.66 band of full-attention diffusion models — while global AR-ness runs 0.88 to 0.97, meaning it mostly generates left to right at the whole-sequence scale even though it need not.

The authors' own limit is the one to hold onto: the clean architectural comparison is a single pair at a single scale, and the models being compared descend from different parents with different tokenisers, so the downstream gaps cannot be assigned to the backbone alone.

glossary.definition: A model trained to recover text from a partially masked sequence, generating by repeatedly unmasking positions rather than appending one token at a time, which allows several positions to be decided in the same pass.

A linear-attention recurrent layer that keeps a fixed-size memory state, edits it with a delta rule that targets specific entries, and gates it to erase quickly; cost per token stays constant as the sequence grows.

The triangular mask that stops an attention layer from looking at later positions. Removing it is what makes a layer bidirectional, and it is available in attention precisely because attention has no inherent direction.

A measure of how left-to-right a diffusion model's generation actually is; local AR-ness looks at neighbouring positions, global AR-ness at the ordering across the whole sequence, and the two can disagree sharply.

foundations.subtitle: Two gases that each refuse to keep reacting, alternated, so film thickness stops being a rate you control and becomes a number you count.
foundations.tldr: Every other deposition process sets thickness with time: pick a rate, pick a duration, hope the rate held. ALD gives that up. It splits one reaction into two halves that each stop when the surface runs out of places to react, so a cycle adds a fixed sub-monolayer no matter how long the gas is left on — and thickness becomes a cycle count, which is the one quantity a machine can hold exactly.

sections.heading: Where thickness-by-time runs out
sections.body_md: Sputtering and chemical vapour deposition both work the same way underneath: atoms arrive at some rate, you wait, you stop. Thickness is rate times time, and the uncertainty in the film is the uncertainty in the rate. That is perfectly adequate at 500 nm and hopeless at 5, because the rate depends on temperature, on how much of the target is left, on gas flow and on where the wafer sits. It also fails for a second reason that has nothing to do with control. If atoms arrive by line of sight, or if they react on contact wherever they land, then the mouth of a deep hole receives more of them than the floor and closes off first. Both failures are failures of a *rate*: something that is fast in one place and slow in another. ALD's move is to arrange for the reaction to have no rate at all — to stop on its own, everywhere, once the surface is used up.
sections.deeper_md: The two problems set the two markets. Thickness control sells ALD into gate dielectrics and DRAM capacitor dielectrics, where a fraction of a nanometre is the specification. Conformality sells it into everything with a high aspect ratio — 3D NAND channels, capacitor holes, spacers for self-aligned multipatterning, where a film must land on a vertical wall as thickly as on a horizontal one.

sections.heading: Two half-reactions that each poison the surface
sections.body_md: Take the canonical process, aluminium oxide from trimethylaluminium and water. Start with a surface carrying hydroxyl groups. Admit trimethylaluminium: it reacts with those OH groups, releasing methane and leaving behind aluminium atoms terminated with methyl groups. Now the important part — trimethylaluminium does not react with a methyl-terminated surface. The moment every hydroxyl is consumed, the reaction stops, and leaving the gas on for ten more seconds or ten more minutes adds nothing. Purge the chamber, admit water, and the reverse happens: water reacts with the methyl groups, releases methane again, and restores a hydroxyl surface, at which point it too has nothing left to attack. Purge again and you are back where you started, one layer thicker. Dose, purge, dose, purge: the whole process is those four steps, repeated. The purges are not housekeeping. If both precursors are in the chamber at once they react with each other in the gas phase, which is ordinary CVD with all of its rate behaviour back.
sections.deeper_md: Written out, the half-reactions are AlOH* + Al(CH₃)₃ → AlOAl(CH₃)₂* + CH₄, then AlOAl(CH₃)₂* + 2H₂O → AlOAl(OH)₂* + 2CH₄, where the asterisk marks a surface species. Both proceed by proton transfer followed by ligand exchange, and both are strongly exothermic, which is why the process runs happily over a wide temperature range. Trimethylaluminium/water is the textbook case partly because it is unusually well-behaved; many processes are considerably less clean, and the ones that matter industrially — hafnium and zirconium oxides from metal-organic precursors, tungsten, titanium nitride — have narrower windows and fussier chemistry.

sections.heading: The saturation curve is the experiment
sections.body_md: Because the claim is that the reaction stops by itself, the measurement that establishes an ALD process is not a thickness — it is a curve. Run a fixed number of cycles at a fixed temperature while stepping only the dose of one precursor, measure the film, and divide by the cycle count to get growth per cycle. Plot growth per cycle against dose. What you want is a curve that rises and then goes flat, because flat means additional precursor changed nothing, which is the operational definition of self-limiting. A curve that keeps climbing means the precursor is doing something other than saturating: decomposing thermally and depositing like CVD, or condensing on a surface that is too cold. You run the same sweep for the second precursor, and then for temperature. Only after all of it does the cycle count mean anything, and it is worth noticing that this is a stronger claim than a process engineer usually gets to make — not that the rate is well controlled, but that the rate no longer exists.
sections.deeper_md: Growth per cycle for real processes runs roughly 0.1 to 2.5 Å per cycle: about 1.0–1.1 Å for Al₂O₃ from trimethylaluminium and water, 0.35–0.45 for TiO₂ from TiCl₄ and water, 1.9 for ZnO from diethylzinc, and 2.5 for tungsten from WF₆ and disilane. Those figures fix the throughput arithmetic — a 20 nm alumina film is roughly 200 cycles, and each cycle carries two purges whose length is set by how long it takes to clear the chamber, not by chemistry. That is why ALD is slow, and why spatial ALD reactors that move the wafer between separated gas zones instead of purging a shared chamber exist at all.

sections.heading: The window, and the four ways out of it
sections.body_md: Self-limiting behaviour only holds over a band of temperatures, and the band is called the ALD window. Go below it and two things can go wrong: the precursor condenses on the surface as a liquid and keeps accumulating, or the reaction is simply too slow to reach saturation in the time you allow. Go above it and two more appear: the precursor decomposes on its own, depositing without waiting for the surface reaction, or the adsorbed species desorbs before the second precursor arrives, so growth per cycle falls. The first pair makes the film too thick, the second pair makes it too thick or too thin depending on which mechanism wins, and all four have the same symptom — growth per cycle stops being flat. Two other departures are worth naming because they are not temperature effects. Growth on an inert starting surface can be delayed for tens of cycles while nucleation sites form, and any process whose ligands decompose slides gradually into CVD-like behaviour without ever looking dramatic.
sections.deeper_md: Nucleation delay is the failure most likely to bite a first-time user, because the tool is behaving correctly and the film is simply not there yet. It is also exploited deliberately: area-selective ALD works by extending nucleation delay on one material with an inhibitor while growth proceeds normally on another, which is how a film gets placed without lithography defining where it goes. The precursor requirements that make all of this possible are unforgiving — vapour pressure above roughly 0.1 Torr so the molecule can be delivered at all, thermal stability across the window so it does not decompose, and enough reactivity with the surface group to saturate in seconds rather than minutes.

sections.heading: A cycle is not a monolayer
sections.body_md: The name promises one atomic layer per cycle and the process does not deliver one, which is the first thing that surprises people and the most instructive. Three effects hold coverage down. The precursor molecule is much larger than the atom it delivers, so once one trimethylaluminium sits on the surface its three methyl groups physically block neighbouring sites — steric hindrance, and it is why bulkier ligands give lower growth per cycle than compact ones. The surface may also simply have fewer reactive groups than it has lattice sites, depending on how it was prepared. And there is a third effect that has nothing to do with chemistry: molecules land one at a time on random sites and stay where they land, so they never settle into the efficient packing a crystallographer would draw. That is random sequential adsorption, and it costs real coverage.
sections.deeper_md: Simulations of random sequential adsorption against ordered packing put the penalty at 22 to 40 percent fewer molecules on the surface for the same precursor. For metallocenes on a hexagonal surface, with precursor radius between 0.5 and 1.0 of the lattice spacing, the gap reaches 40 percent; for cobaltocene on Co(0001), where the molecule is large relative to the lattice, it narrows to 22 percent. The practical consequence is that growth per cycle is not predictable from molecular geometry alone, and that a chemistry which looks like it should deposit a monolayer will not, no matter how long the dose.

sections.heading: Getting a film to the bottom of a 900-to-1 hole
sections.body_md: Here is where the self-limiting property pays for its slowness. In a deep hole, molecules reach the floor by bouncing down the walls, and the ones that stick on the way never arrive. Any process with a rate coats the top faster and pinches the opening shut. In ALD the top saturates and then stops accepting anything, so molecules that would have stuck there are reflected further down. Keep dosing and the saturation front works its way to the bottom. The film ends up the same thickness everywhere; you pay for it in exposure, not in uniformity. The bill is steep and it is quadratic: the dose needed to saturate a hole scales with the square of its aspect ratio. Double the depth and you need four times the exposure. That is the trade in one line, and it is why ALD is used where nothing else works rather than wherever a film is wanted.
sections.deeper_md: The regime is set by s₀·AR², where s₀ is the initial sticking probability, typically 10⁻⁵ to 10⁻¹. Below 1 the growth is reaction-limited and conformality is easy; above about 100 it is diffusion-limited and the saturation dose follows Gordon's 2003 result, proportional to AR²/A₀ with A₀ the area per adsorption site. Plasma ALD changes the picture in a way worth knowing: a plasma supplies radicals rather than a stable molecule, and radicals recombine on the sidewalls. The distinction Arts, Kessels and Knoops draw is that adsorption loss stops once a surface saturates, while recombination loss never stops — so recombination, not sticking, is what limits plasma ALD in deep features. With a recombination probability near 6 × 10⁻⁵, plasma ALD of SiO₂ and TiO₂ has been coated conformally to aspect ratios around 900 by extending the plasma step.

glossary.definition: The thickness added by one complete ALD cycle, usually quoted in ångströms. It is a property of the chemistry, the surface and the temperature, and its constancy across dose is what makes the process ALD rather than CVD.

A surface reaction that consumes the sites it needs and then cannot proceed further, so more precursor changes nothing. Both halves of an ALD cycle must be self-limiting; if either is not, thickness depends on dose again.

The temperature band over which both half-reactions stay self-limiting. Below it precursors condense or react too slowly; above it they decompose or desorb. The symptom of leaving it in any direction is that growth per cycle stops being flat.

The groups attached to the metal atom in a precursor — the three methyls on trimethylaluminium, for instance. They make the molecule volatile enough to deliver, they terminate the surface and stop the reaction, and their bulk is what keeps growth per cycle below a monolayer.

The inert-gas flush between the two precursor doses. Its job is to ensure the two precursors never meet in the gas phase, because if they do the process reverts to CVD; purge time is usually what sets ALD's throughput.

The ratio of film thickness at the bottom of a feature to thickness at the top. ALD reaches close to 1 because saturation stops deposition at the mouth of a feature and lets later molecules travel further in.

The chance that a precursor molecule arriving at a bare surface site reacts rather than bouncing away, typically 10⁻⁵ to 10⁻¹. A low value is bad for speed and good for conformality, because an unreactive molecule travels deeper before it commits.
Depth divided by width for a hole or trench. It appears squared in the ALD dose requirement, which is the reason a 900:1 structure is coatable at all and also the reason it takes so long.

foundations.try_this: Run the saturation experiment on a tool the club already owns. Spin-coat a series of wafers at one speed for one time, stepping only the dispensed resist volume from clearly too little up to plainly excessive, and measure the resulting thickness on each. Plot thickness against volume rather than against speed. If the curve flattens, you have found the point past which the process stopped caring about how much you gave it — the same shape as an ALD saturation curve, and the same thing it is claiming. Then read section 2 of Li, Chai and Wang and write down the one difference that matters: an ALD half-reaction is flat in dose *and* in exposure time, which is what converts a rate into a count. Pair it with Van Zant chapter 12 on deposition for where ALD sits among the other film processes the club can actually run.
